Plain itself is built on this same GraphQL API. This means that there are no limitations in what can be done via the API vs the UI. These docs cover the most used operations. For anything not documented here, read the schema or get in touch . If you’re looking to access our GraphQL API from an Agent, try our MCP Server instead. For TypeScript, the GraphQL SDK gives you a fully typed client for these operations. Key details Our API is compatible with all common GraphQL clients with the following details: API URL: https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1 Allowed method : POST Required headers: Content-Type: application/json Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN where the token is your API key. See authentication for more details. JSON body: query : the GraphQL query string variables : a JSON object of variables used in the GraphQL query operationName : the name of your GraphQL operation (used for tracking only; it does not affect the call or its result) If you’d like to use the GraphQL schema to generate types for your client code you can fetch the schema from: https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1/schema.graphql Your first API call In this example, we’re going to get a customer in your workspace by their email address. You can find a customer’s email on the right-hand side when looking at one of their threads in Plain. You will need an API key with the customer:read permission. See authentication for details on how to get an API key You’ll need to set two shell variables: PLAIN_TOKEN : The API key PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL : The email of the customer you want to fetch PLAIN_TOKEN = XXX PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL = XXX curl -X POST https://core-api.uk.plain.com/graphql/v1 \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $PLAIN_TOKEN " \ -d '{"query":"query customerByEmail($email: String!) { customerByEmail(email: $email) { id fullName updatedAt { iso8601 } } }","variables":{"email":"'" $PLAIN_CUSTOMER_EMAIL "'"},"operationName":"customerByEmail"}' Was this page helpful? A machine user can have several API keys, so you can rotate them without downtime. Each API key carries its own fine-grained permissions. To call the API as a user in your workspace, use an OAuth app . 1 Create a machine user Go to Settings → Machine users & agents and click Add machine user . Pick API User and click Continue . Pick Agent instead if you’re building an agent . A machine user has two fields: Name: visible only to you and could indicate the usage e.g. “Autoresponder” Public name: This is the name visible to customers (if the machine user interacts with customers) e.g. “Mr Robot” 2 Create an API Key Click “Add API key” and select the permissions you need. When making API calls, if you have insufficient permissions, the error should tell you which permissions you need. The relevant documentation will tell you which permissions are required for each feature. Once you’ve made an API key you should copy it and put it somewhere safe, as you will not be able to see it again once you navigate away. 3 Go build things 🚀 Now that you have an API key, pass it on any API call as a header: Authorization: Bearer plainApiKey_xxx Was this page helpful? pages.text: OAuth - Plain Docs Documentation Index Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further. Skip to main content Assistant Responses are generated using AI and may contain mistakes. Plain Docs home page Search... ⌘ K Ask Assistant ⌘ I Help Center Changelog Blog Search... Navigation GraphQL API OAuth Documentation Developer API Reference GraphQL API Introduction Authentication OAuth Schema Pagination Error handling Error codes Customers Accounts Threads Tiers SLA policies Business hours Reporting Events Labels Messaging Snippets Tasks Knowledge gaps AI feedback Notes Webhook targets Discussions Help center Building your own ticket importer Attachments API explorer GraphQL SDK Building Agents Getting started Interacting in Discussions Working on Threads Tool Calls Suggesting Replies Working with Notes Using Knowledge Examples Agent integrations Overview MCP server Agent skill Cursor Webhooks Overview Webhook Versions Webhook events Webhooks SDK Channels Authentication Headless portal Custom channels Customer Cards Overview Create a customer card Protocol Playground Examples UI Components Overview Badge Container CopyButton Divider LinkButton WorkflowButton PlainText Row Spacer Text UI components SDK Security Request signing mTLS IP Addresses Changelog Changelog On this page Back to top Choose an OAuth app type Create an OAuth app Allowed origins for a client-side app Get an access token Call the API Disable or delete an OAuth app GraphQL API OAuth Call the API as a user in your workspace after they sign in to your OAuth app. An OAuth app lets users in your workspace sign in to your app with their Plain account. Your app then calls the API as that user, with the permissions their role already has, and Plain records those actions as that user. To call the API as an integration rather than as a user, create a machine user instead. Choose an OAuth app type The OAuth app type determines how your app authenticates when it exchanges an authorization code for an access token. Pick the type before you create the app, because you can’t change it afterwards: Client-side : your app exchanges the code in a browser or a mobile or desktop app, where a secret wouldn’t stay secret. The app has no client secret and must use Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE). Server-side : your app exchanges the code from your backend, where you can keep a secret. Plain creates a client secret for the app and shows it once. PKCE proves that the token request comes from the app that started the sign-in. Your app generates a random code verifier, sends its SHA-256 hash as the code challenge when the user signs in, then sends the verifier itself with the authorization code. To switch types, create a new OAuth app and move your integration to it. Create an OAuth app Creating an OAuth app gives you a client ID, which identifies your app to Plain and isn’t secret. A server-side app also gets a client secret. 1 Open the form Go to Settings → OAuth applications and click Add OAuth app . 2 Fill in the form The form has these fields: App name : The name users see when they sign in. Description : Optional. OAuth app type : Client-side or Server-side . The form selects Client-side by default. Redirect URLs : Where Plain sends a user after they sign in. Put each URL on its own line. Allowed origins : Shown only for a client-side app. See Allowed origins for a client-side app . Each redirect URL and allowed origin must use HTTPS, or HTTP on localhost . 3 Create the app Click Create OAuth app . For a client-side app, Plain opens the app’s settings page, which shows the client ID. For a server-side app, Plain first shows the client ID and client secret. Click Done to open the app’s settings page. Copy the client secret before you click Done . You can’t see it again. If you lose it, create a new server-side app. The list in Settings → OAuth applications shows each app’s type, and so does the Credentials card on the app’s settings page. Allowed origins for a client-side app An allowed origin is a website that may call Plain’s sign-in endpoints, such as the token endpoint, from the browser. A client-side app needs at least one, because it exchanges the code from the browser, and the browser blocks the call from any other origin. Write each origin on its own line as a scheme and host, with an optional port and no path, such as https://app.example.com or http://localhost:3000 . A server-side app exchanges the code from your backend, so the create form doesn’t ask for allowed origins. Get an access token Your app gets an access token with the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow: it sends the user to sign in, receives a code at a redirect URL, and exchanges that code for tokens. The authorization server is https://signin.auth.plain.com , and its OpenID configuration lists the endpoints. 1 Send the user to sign in Redirect the user to the authorize endpoint with these query parameters: client_id : Your app’s client ID. redirect_uri : One of the app’s redirect URLs. response_type : code . scope : openid , plus offline_access if you want a refresh token. state and nonce : Random values you generate for this sign-in. Check that the state Plain returns matches the one you sent. code_challenge and code_challenge_method : The PKCE code challenge, with method S256 . A client-side app must send these. A server-side app can skip PKCE, but we recommend it. This builds the URL in TypeScript: const params = new URLSearchParams ({ client_id: 'your_client_id' , redirect_uri: 'your_redirect_url' , response_type: 'code' , scope: 'openid offline_access' , state: 'your_state' , nonce: 'your_nonce' , code_challenge: 'your_code_challenge' , code_challenge_method: 'S256' , }); const authorizeUrl = `https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/authorize? ${ params } ` ; A user in more than one workspace chooses which workspace to sign in to. The app only works in the workspace you created it in. 2 Exchange the code for tokens After the user signs in, Plain redirects to redirect_uri with a code . Exchange it at the token endpoint, https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token . For a server-side app, send the client secret from your backend. This request also sends the code verifier, because it used PKCE: curl -X POST https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token \ -d client_id=your_client_id \ -d client_secret=your_client_secret \ -d grant_type=authorization_code \ -d code=your_authorization_code \ -d redirect_uri=your_redirect_url \ -d code_verifier=your_code_verifier For a client-side app, send the code verifier and no client secret. The page’s origin must be one of the app’s allowed origins: const tokenUrl = 'https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token' ; const response = await fetch ( tokenUrl , { method: 'POST' , body: new URLSearchParams ({ client_id: 'your_client_id' , grant_type: 'authorization_code' , code: 'your_authorization_code' , redirect_uri: 'your_redirect_url' , code_verifier: 'your_code_verifier' , }), }); The response includes these fields: access_token : The token you send to the API. expires_in : How many seconds the access token lasts. refresh_token : Included when the sign-in requested offline_access . 3 Refresh the access token Before the access token expires, send the refresh token to the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token and the client ID. A server-side app also sends its client secret: curl -X POST https://signin.auth.plain.com/oauth2/token \ -d client_id=your_client_id \ -d client_secret=your_client_secret \ -d grant_type=refresh_token \ -d refresh_token=your_refresh_token Store the refresh token from each response and use it for the next refresh. Call the API The API URL and request body are the same as for an API key; see Key details . Send the access token in the same header an API key uses: Authorization: Bearer your_access_token Each query and mutation runs as the signed-in user, with their current role. Changing their role changes what the app can do, and removing them from the workspace stops the app working for them. If they lack a permission, the error names it. GraphQL subscriptions don’t accept OAuth app tokens. The API rejects a token from a disabled or deleted app, or from another workspace, with HTTP status 401 and the error code UNAUTHENTICATED . The error doesn’t say which of these applies. Disable or delete an OAuth app Disabling an OAuth app stops it without losing its settings. On the app’s settings page, turn off Enabled in the Status card and click Save changes . Users can’t sign in to the app, and the API rejects every request from it, including tokens issued before you disabled it, until you enable it again. To delete the app, use the Delete card on its settings page. Deleting an OAuth app ends its access immediately. You can’t undo a delete. Was this page helpful? Navigation Building Agents Set up an agent Documentation Developer API Reference GraphQL API Introduction Authentication OAuth Schema Pagination Error handling Error codes Customers Accounts Threads Tiers SLA policies Business hours Reporting Events Labels Messaging Snippets Tasks Knowledge gaps AI feedback Notes Webhook targets Discussions Help center Building your own ticket importer Attachments API explorer GraphQL SDK Building Agents Getting started Interacting in Discussions Working on Threads Tool Calls Suggesting Replies Working with Notes Using Knowledge Examples Agent integrations Overview MCP server Agent skill Cursor Webhooks Overview Webhook Versions Webhook events Webhooks SDK Channels Authentication Headless portal Custom channels Customer Cards Overview Create a customer card Protocol Playground Examples UI Components Overview Badge Container CopyButton Divider LinkButton WorkflowButton PlainText Row Spacer Text UI components SDK Security Request signing mTLS IP Addresses Changelog Changelog On this page Back to top Building your agent Building Agents Set up an agent Create a machine user for your agent, give it an API key, and start receiving events from Plain. An agent you build and connect to Plain is a connected agent. Each discussion or thread assignment by your agent uses 15 credits. See How credits work . To build an agent in Plain, at a high level you have to: 1 Create a machine user Go to Agents and click Add agent under Connected agents . This creates a machine user with the type Agent , which is the type for any agent you build. You can also go to Settings → Machine users & agents and click Add machine user . Plain asks what kind of machine user to make: pick Agent , or API User for integrations that only call the API, then click Continue . Name is only visible to your team, for example “Billing agent” Public name is what customers see when the agent replies, for example “Acme Support” The avatar is shown to you internally and, if your agent interacts with customers, publicly as well. Create one machine user per agent. 2 Create an API key Click Add API key and grant the permissions the agent needs. Each page in this section lists the permissions for its calls. A mutation without the right permission returns an error that names the missing one. Plain shows the key once, so you should copy it when it is created. A machine user can hold more than one key, so you can rotate without downtime. Read more on GraphQL authentication 3 Set up webhooks Go to Settings → Webhooks and click Add webhook target . Point it at an HTTPS endpoint you control and subscribe to the events you need. You can update these later as you build your agent. Read more on working with webhooks . Building your agent With the above basic steps, you can now build your agent. Agents can do anything in Plain. You should pick where you want to start based on the use case for your agent. Assisting your team Make your agent available to your team directly within Plain to chat and assist them. Doing support autonomously Let your agent handle threads autonomously end to end. Navigation Agent integrations MCP server Documentation Developer API Reference GraphQL API Introduction Authentication OAuth Schema Pagination Error handling Error codes Customers Accounts Threads Tiers SLA policies Business hours Reporting Events Labels Messaging Snippets Tasks Knowledge gaps AI feedback Notes Webhook targets Discussions Help center Building your own ticket importer Attachments API explorer GraphQL SDK Building Agents Getting started Interacting in Discussions Working on Threads Tool Calls Suggesting Replies Working with Notes Using Knowledge Examples Agent integrations Overview MCP server Agent skill Cursor Webhooks Overview Webhook Versions Webhook events Webhooks SDK Channels Authentication Headless portal Custom channels Customer Cards Overview Create a customer card Protocol Playground Examples UI Components Overview Badge Container CopyButton Divider LinkButton WorkflowButton PlainText Row Spacer Text UI components SDK Security Request signing mTLS IP Addresses Changelog Changelog On this page Back to top Setup ChatGPT Cursor Claude.ai Claude Code FX Other MCP clients Authentication Required OAuth scopes Available tools Good to know Interactive views in your chat Thread Workflow editor Labels Which clients show views Use case examples Triage your queue Understand a customer’s history Summarize what’s waiting Draft a reply with full context Audit your Help Center Fill a knowledge gap Get a snapshot of an account’s health Cross-reference with other tools If something isn’t working Agent integrations MCP server Connect Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client to your Plain workspace over the Model Context Protocol. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI tools connect to external platforms. The Plain MCP server at https://mcp.plain.com/mcp lets tools like Claude, ChatGPT, and Cursor work with your support data directly. You authenticate with your existing Plain account, so the MCP server has the same permissions as your user. No API keys needed. Setup ChatGPT In ChatGPT, add the official Plain plugin: Open the Plain plugin and add it Sign in with your Plain account and choose your workspace In a chat, type @ and pick Plain Cursor You can add the Plain MCP to Cursor via your Cursor config at ~/.cursor/mcp.json { "mcpServers" : { "plain" : { "type" : "remote" , "url" : "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp" } } } Go to Cursor Settings → Tools & MCP and click Connect next to Plain to authenticate. Claude.ai Go to “Customize” → “Connectors” Click the ➕ icon, then choose “Add custom connector” Add a custom connector named “Plain” with the Remote MCP server URL https://mcp.plain.com/mcp Click the “Connect” button next to the newly created Plain connector to authenticate. If you’re on a Claude Team plan, you may need to reach out to your administrator to add this custom connector for you. Claude Code Adding the Plain MCP to claude-code can be done via the mcp-remote helper package which involves adding the following to your ~/.claude.json configuration. "mcpServers" : { "plain" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "-y" , "mcp-remote" , "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp" ], "enabled" : true } } Unfortunately Claude Code does not support refreshing OAuth tokens yet. A workaround until that is implemented is to use the mcp-remote npm package. Next time you start Claude Code, it will launch a browser window asking you to authenticate with your Plain account and select the workspace you’d like to connect. Run the /mcp command and select the plain MCP to see more details. FX fx is a terminal AI coding agent from Vercel Labs. Add the Plain MCP via the CLI: fx mcp add --transport http plain https://mcp.plain.com/mcp Or add it manually to ~/.fx/mcp.json : { "mcp": { "plain": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.plain.com/mcp", "enabled": true } } } fx will prompt you to complete the OAuth flow with your Plain account on the next session start. Other MCP clients MCP clients that run locally (not in the browser) can connect to Plain if they support remote HTTP servers. Point it at https://mcp.plain.com/mcp and complete the OAuth flow when prompted. Authentication Plain MCP uses OAuth to allow your MCP server connection to share the same context as your normal web app user. No additional managing of permissions required. This means replies to threads will appear as though they come from your user. Required OAuth scopes The Plain MCP server requires every OAuth token to include the openid and offline_access scopes. If your authorization request omits these, the server returns 403 Forbidden , even when OAuth completes successfully and returns tokens. Set scope to openid offline_access (space-separated) in your authorization request. If you are using @modelcontextprotocol/sdk , some versions discover required scopes automatically via the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint . If yours does not, set them explicitly in your client configuration. After you sign in, your client receives an access token and a refresh token; automatic refresh depends on your client. Available tools Once connected, your AI client can do almost anything you can do in Plain, across nearly 400 tools. Tools cover: Threads and replies Customers and accounts Labels, thread fields, and tasks The Help Center and knowledge sources Workflows and broadcasts Tiers, service level agreements (SLAs), and business hours Snippets and saved views Discussions with the Sidekick Agent Good to know Your AI client can ask you to confirm actions such as sending a reply or deleting data. Your Plain role and permissions apply to every tool. Some changes stay in the Plain app: API keys, billing, roles, invites, webhooks, and custom domains. The tool list can change. Reconnect the server if a tool is missing. Interactive views in your chat Some AI clients can show parts of Plain right inside the chat, so you can review and change what your AI client set up without opening Plain. These views are built on MCP Apps , an official extension to MCP. They act as your user, with your role and permissions, like every other tool. Your AI client opens a view by calling one of the tools below. AI clients call these tools when they’re relevant, for example after creating a workflow or when a specific thread comes up. You can also ask for one directly: “Show me my labels.” Thread showThread shows a thread as Plain’s thread page. You can read the thread’s messages, reply, add notes, and change the thread’s status, assignee, priority, labels and fields. The view doesn’t update live; it refreshes every 15s while it’s on screen. Workflow editor showWorkflow opens a workflow in Plain’s workflow editor, so you can review and change a workflow your AI client built or changed. Labels showLabels shows your workspace’s labels , which you can create and edit in place. Your AI client can pass labels it recommends as suggestions, and you create the ones you want by clicking them. The call itself creates nothing. Which clients show views Views appear in clients that support the MCP Apps extension, for example Claude.ai, Claude Desktop and ChatGPT. For the current list, see the MCP extension support matrix . In clients without MCP Apps support, the view tools aren’t listed. Every other tool works as usual and returns text, so there’s nothing to set up. Use case examples Triage your queue “Show me my assigned threads. Summarize the top 5 by urgency and suggest which ones I should handle first.” Read your active threads and get a prioritized summary without opening each one. Understand a customer’s history “Look up the customer with email alex@acme.com . Show me their recent threads and summarize the pattern. Are they hitting the same issue repeatedly?” Pull together a customer’s full context in seconds instead of clicking through timelines. Summarize what’s waiting “Show me all my TODO threads. Group them by label and summarize what each one is about.” See what has gone quiet, so you can decide what needs attention. Draft a reply with full context “Show me thread th_01ABC123. Read the full timeline, then draft a reply that addresses the customer’s latest question. Use a helpful but concise tone.” The AI reads the full thread history and drafts a reply for you to review before sending. Audit your Help Center “List all articles in my Help Center. Flag any that haven’t been updated in the last 90 days.” Spot outdated documentation without manually checking each article. Fill a knowledge gap “Show me the knowledge gaps customers hit this week. For the top one, check whether our knowledge sources already cover it, draft a Help Center article, and mark the gap’s task done.” Turn a question the Customer Agent couldn’t answer into an article without leaving your AI client. Get a snapshot of an account’s health “Look up the account ‘Acme Corp’. Show me their details and all open threads. Are there any patterns or escalation risks?” Prep for an account review by pulling account context and open issues together. Cross-reference with other tools The Plain MCP works alongside other MCP servers. If you also have Slack, GitHub, or Linear MCPs connected, you can combine them: “Find threads about ‘payment errors’ from the last 7 days, check if there’s a related GitHub issue, and post a summary to #incidents in Slack.” Each server handles its own domain, and the AI coordinates between them. If something isn’t working Can’t authenticate: Make sure you can log into Plain at app.plain.com first. The MCP server uses the same auth. 403 after OAuth completes: Your token is missing required scopes. Add openid offline_access to the scope parameter in your authorization request and complete a fresh OAuth flow. See Authentication for details. Tool not appearing: Some AI clients cache available tools. Try disconnecting and reconnecting the MCP server. View not appearing: Check that your client supports MCP Apps (see Which clients show views ). If it does, disconnect and reconnect the Plain MCP server, then start a new chat. Permission errors: Check that your Plain user has the right role for the action you’re trying to take. If it’s still not working, collect: Your workspace ID (visible in Settings → General ) The exact error message Which AI client you’re using Then reach out to us via help@plain.com for assistance. The chat widget treats a customer as anonymous until you prove who they are. Pick one of 3 approaches: Display fields : show a name and avatar for an anonymous customer Signature : sign a signed-in customer’s email and identifiers on your server Email verification : ask the customer to verify an email in the widget Pass display fields A customer is anonymous until you provide and prove an email. You can still pass display fields on customerDetails in Plain.init . Plain doesn’t treat those fields as proof of who the customer is: Plain . init ({ customerDetails: { fullName: 'Ada Lovelace' , shortName: 'Ada' , chatAvatarUrl: 'https://example.com/avatars/ada.png' , }, }); Sign a known customer Use this when the customer is already signed in to your product and you know their email. The signature covers the email, plus externalId and tenantIdentifier when you send them. externalId is your ID for the customer. tenantIdentifier is { tenantId: 'ten_0123456789' } or { externalId: 'acme' } for their account . 1 Generate a chat secret Go to Settings → Chat , open the chat app, and click Generate secret . Keep the secret on your server, never in the browser. Clicking Re-generate secret invalidates the current secret, and signatures from the old secret stop verifying. 2 Build the signature on your server The signature is a Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC). Sign the message with HMAC-SHA256 and your chat secret, then hex-encode the digest. With no externalId and no tenantIdentifier , the message is the email itself: ada@example.com With either identifier, the message is JSON. Sort the keys alphabetically at every level, and set v to the number 1 : {"email":"ada@example.com","identifiers":{"externalId":"user_123","tenantIdentifier":{"externalId":"acme"}},"v":1} This TypeScript example builds that message and returns the signature. JSON.stringify drops identifiers you leave undefined and keeps the key order shown: import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto' ; type TenantIdentifier = { tenantId : string } | { externalId : string }; function customerDetailsSignature ( args : { secret : string ; email : string ; externalId ?: string ; tenantIdentifier ?: TenantIdentifier ; }) : string { const { secret , email , externalId , tenantIdentifier } = args ; const message = externalId === undefined && tenantIdentifier === undefined ? email : JSON . stringify ({ email , identifiers: { externalId , tenantIdentifier }, v: 1 , }); return createHmac ( 'sha256' , secret ). update ( message ). digest ( 'hex' ); } Test vectors Compare your function to these signatures. Each one uses the secret chat_secret_example . Each block shows the exact message, then its lowercase hex signature. A space or line break in the message changes the signature. Sign ada@example.com with no identifiers: message: ada@example.com signature: ad990bba2bd71e79e79c042c6291344ae152fa267d6c15446b2e97b2892834df Sign ada@example.com and externalId user_123 : message: {"email":"ada@example.com","identifiers":{"externalId":"user_123"},"v":1} signature: 07c1924d9865df9b1cefceedebd61dfd1b2b25ac790389ea56e5eb005fce660d Sign ada@example.com and tenantIdentifier { externalId: 'acme' } : message: {"email":"ada@example.com","identifiers":{"tenantIdentifier":{"externalId":"acme"}},"v":1} signature: d5932983b7a19f4f167407c3b47977be3f0558289a964ab1fc1160dadd4aa0dc Sign ada@example.com and tenantIdentifier { tenantId: 'ten_0123456789' } : message: {"email":"ada@example.com","identifiers":{"tenantIdentifier":{"tenantId":"ten_0123456789"}},"v":1} signature: 7441bdf9502fd332a92e7b657c5908c44e9602c40ad650692313d82f4f55c0fa Sign ada@example.com , externalId user_123 , and tenantIdentifier { externalId: 'acme' } : message: {"email":"ada@example.com","identifiers":{"externalId":"user_123","tenantIdentifier":{"externalId":"acme"}},"v":1} signature: bd90fca5ec85587de6f5e92f097720477f1648bd42d3983c27c17bea3df2eb66 3 Pass the details and signature to the widget Pass customerDetailsSignature next to customerDetails . The values in customerDetails must match the ones you signed. In this example, fetchCustomerFromBackend calls your own endpoint, which returns { customerDetails, customerDetailsSignature } for the signed-in customer, so the details and the signature come from one place. const { customerDetails , customerDetailsSignature } = await fetchCustomerFromBackend (); Plain . init ({ customerDetails , customerDetailsSignature , }); Fetch a new payload when the email or the identifiers change. Plain rejects the request when externalId or tenantIdentifier differs from what you signed. The signature is a bearer credential: anyone who has it can claim that customer. Verify an unknown email Set requireAuthentication when the customer isn’t signed in and you want an email before they can chat. This fits a public page where you don’t manage sign-in. You can pair this option with the Require email verification setting in Settings → Chat . Plain . init ({ requireAuthentication: true , }); The widget asks for an email address. Plain emails a one-time code. After the customer enters the code, they can start a thread . Was this page helpful? A machine user can have several API keys, so you can rotate them without downtime. Each API key carries its own fine-grained permissions. To call the API as a user in your workspace, use an OAuth app . 1 Create a machine user Go to Settings → Machine users & agents and click Add machine user . Pick API User and click Continue . Pick Agent instead if you’re building an agent . A machine user has two fields: Name: visible only to you and could indicate the usage e.g. “Autoresponder” Public name: This is the name visible to customers (if the machine user interacts with customers) e.g. “Mr Robot” 2 Create an API Key Click “Add API key” and select the permissions you need. When making API calls, if you have insufficient permissions, the error should tell you which permissions you need. The relevant documentation will tell you which permissions are required for each feature. Once you’ve made an API key you should copy it and put it somewhere safe, as you will not be able to see it again once you navigate away. 3 Go build things 🚀 Now that you have an API key, pass it on any API call as a header: Authorization: Bearer plainApiKey_xxx Was this page helpful?
